newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Volvo, Mitsubishi in truck talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Volvo, Mitsubishi in truck talks.

text.p: A proposal to tighten the links between Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo and Japan's Mitsubishi Corp in trucks was seen as a positive step for both companies by analysts on Monday.

The two companies, which already have a joint venture car production plant in The Netherlands called NedCar, have agreed to look at ways to cooperate on truck operations in Europe and Asia and expand their bases.
"We will do a pre-study and then we will make a decision," Volvo spokesman Stefan Lorentzson told Reuters.
"We are looking at all possibilites and that goes for production, product development and distribution."
Analysts said the proposal, outlined last week, came as no real surprise as auto companies worldwide were looking at ways to boost competitiveness and enter new markets.
"Volvo clearly has good relations with Mitsubishi and they have always said that they would look at ways and means to develop the businesses and reduce costs," said BZW analyst Philip Ayton.
"The truck business has got tougher in Europe and is becoming more global and more competitive so this is probably the right time for this move."

After a record year in 1995, Volvo Truck has suffered this year due to its loss-making U.S. operations where falling sales have dragged global sales in the first 10 months of the year down to 53,170 from 63,260 a year ago.
With new management now in place in the U.S. and after closing a plant in Ohio and cutting its workforce by 10 percent, Volvo has turned its attention to other areas.
Volvo Truck is the second largest division in the company, accounting for about 30 percent of sales and around 68 percent of operating income.
Lorentzson said the exact details of the agreement had yet to be hammered out.

One possibility could be for Volvo to use Mitsubishi's distribution network in Asia while the Japanese company takes advantage of Volvo's European network to sell its Canter pick-up truck that it started to make in Portugal this August.
"We are interested in going deeper into Asia and they, Mitsubishi, want to do the same in Europe," Lorentzon said.
Analyst Francois Colli from Paribas said Volvo and Mitsubishi's trucks complemented each other.
While Volvo is one of the world's largest producers of heavy vehicles, weighing 16 tonnes and above, Mitsubishi concentrates on medium weight vehicle of six to 16 tonnes.
In 1995 Volvo Truck delivered 76,500 heavy and medium-heavy trucks with 35 percent to the U.S., 46 percent in Europe and only 19 percent to other markets including Asia.
"I think a closer agreement will be positive for both Volvo and Mitsubishi," Colli told Reuters.
"In the auto business there is more and more cooperation because of a greater need to increase volumes and to share product development costs for economies of scale.
"If they could finalise an agreement to share new product development costs, distribution, and also products, possibly in Asia, this would be good news."

Volvo and Mitsubishi already have a good track record of cooperation, with the agreement Volvo's main joint venture after it dropped plans to merger with Renault in 1994. Volvo now has a strategy to be a stand-alone manufacturer.
The NedCar plant, set up in 1989, is owned in three equal parts by the carmakers and the Dutch government. It produces the medium-size Volvo S40/V40 range and Mitsubishi's Carisma.
The two companies have also linked over Mitsubishi's newly developed fuel-efficient gasoline injection engines (GDI).
